title: Thousands of US flights cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide

 21 minutes ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Sakshi Venkatraman and James FitzGerald 'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop US officials and airlines have signalled a return to normality for air travel from Monday, after a weekend of disruption as the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop.
 Speaking on Sunday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said: "As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity."
 American Airlines has said it plans to operate "a largely normal schedule" from Monday, after thousands of flight delays and cancellations nationwide since Friday.
 An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.
 In his comments on Sunday, Duffy explained to the BBC's US partner CBS News that the after-effects meant it would take time for things to return to normal. 
 "We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time." 
 Every US airline was affected by Friday's ground stop, which lasted for more than four hours. The total number of flight cancellations had topped 17,000 by Sunday, according to Bloomberg, which cited aviation data providers.
 Thousands of other flights were delayed. The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. 
 The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.
 In its update on Sunday evening, American Airlines also said: "We are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event."
 Some other major US carriers gave updates of their own earlier the same day. 
 Delta Air Lines said: "While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations."
 Alaska Airlines said its operations, and those of Hawaiian Airlines, had "mostly recovered", though thousands of people were still trying to reach their destinations.
 Getty Images The issue occurred during an attempt to update part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.
 In the wake of the chaos, Duffy has issued calls for a wider upgrade of the technology, to the tune of tens of billions of dollars. 
 He and President Donald Trump have urged Congress to approve more money for modernisation work to take place. Debate has turned to whether or not funds already approved by Congress are sufficient for the purpose.
 Duffy told CBS that Congress had been "very specific" about existing funding, which was "all spent". He added: "What I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software." 
 Speaking to the same network, Jim Himes, a congressman from the opposition Democratic Party, said: "This is not a Congress money problem." Instead, he argued, it was "a prioritisation problem".
 How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
 Investigators are still working to determine the root cause of the issue and who might have been at fault.
 In his account of what happened, Duffy said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals. 
 The router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was in El Dorado, Arkansas. The signals "flooded our network", he said. 
 Duffy said that issues would continue to arise until the US made major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said.
 "Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."
 In his own comments, delivered in a post on Truth Social, Trump urged US lawmakers to allocate money for such a project, saying "we can get it built quickly and efficiently".
 "It will be the BEST SYSTEM anywhere in the World. Much of our current air control system is 50 years old - RIDICULOUS! We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs," he said. 
 Experts say the technology used by the US for flight communications is antiquated. 
 Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described it as "a house that's about to be condemned".
 He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."
